extraction.name: MathQA
extraction.description: MathQA is a large-scale dataset of 37,200 English multiple-choice math word problems annotated with formal operation programs. It enhances the AQuA dataset by providing fully-specified operational programs across multiple math domain categories including geometry, physics, probability, and others. The dataset is designed to support interpretable neural math problem solving.
extraction.creator: Aida Amini (University of Washington); Saadia Gabriel (University of Washington); Shanchuan Lin (University of Washington); Rik Koncel-Kedziorski (University of Washington); Yejin Choi (University of Washington; Allen Institute for AI); Hannaneh Hajishirzi (University of Washington; Allen Institute for AI)
extraction.citeAs: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, and Hannaneh Hajishirzi. 2019. MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms. arXiv:1905.13319.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The MathQA dataset was constructed by taking math word problems from the existing AQuA dataset and annotating them with formal operation programs using a crowdsourcing platform (Figure Eight). Annotators iteratively selected operations and arguments via a dynamic annotation platform, and annotations were validated by at least 2 out of 3 validators. Annotation expansion was also performed by finding closely similar problems using Levenshtein distance and extending annotations to cover more problems.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis; Manual Human Curator; User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Many AQuA problems were excluded as unsolvable or noisy: problems with no words (37 train), sequence problems (1,991 train), problems requiring options (6,643 train), non-numeric problems (10,227 train), and near-duplicates (17,294 train). Only 65,991 of 97,467 AQuA training problems were deemed solvable. Additionally, automatic annotation via dynamic programming was attempted but only 61% of those problems passed human validation, so automatic annotations were excluded.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The AQuA-RAT dataset (Ling et al., 2017), which contains over 100K GRE- and GMAT-level multiple-choice math word problems with rationales, served as the source data. Problems were filtered for solvability, removing duplicates, sequence problems, non-numeric problems, and problems requiring options or brute-force enumeration.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd workers annotated math word problems with formal operation programs using a dynamic annotation platform. Annotators were provided with a problem description, a list of operations related to the problem category, and a list of valid arguments. They iteratively selected operations and arguments until the problem was solved. Quality control was enforced via randomly evaluated test questions; annotators had to maintain an accuracy threshold, and those falling below it had their annotations marked as untrusted and re-queued. A validation strategy required at least 2 out of 3 validators to rank an operation program as valid for it to be accepted.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Validation accuracy was 94.64% across categories. Expert evaluation of 500 problems showed 92% of annotations were valid, with 87% agreement between expert validation and the crowdsourcing validation task. For categorization, human annotator agreement was 84% and their agreement with the model was 74.5%.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: OpenNMT; automatic dynamic programming approach for generating operation programs; Levenshtein distance for annotation expansion
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The AQuA dataset contains statistical bias that the representation language aims to reduce; categorization strategy may be noisy due to use of only one mathematical interpretation for each domain-specific n-gram
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Omits high-order polynomials and problems where solutions are entirely nonnumeric; representation language does not cover all operation types (e.g., factorization); sequence problems and problems requiring brute-force reasoning are beyond current scope; some problems in AQuA are near-duplicates, have incorrect solutions, or are unsolvable without brute-force enumeration
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training and evaluation of neural models for math word problem solving; benchmarking interpretable math problem solvers; research on logical reasoning over natural language
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Annotation expansion was performed by finding closely similar problems using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words in edit distance, replacing numeric values with generic numbers, and expanding annotations to cover more problems from the AQuA dataset.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems from the AQuA dataset were filtered for solvability, removing problems with no words, sequence problems, problems requiring options, non-numeric problems, and near-duplicates. Math problems were categorized into math domains using term frequencies. The dataset was randomly split into 80/12/8% training/dev/test problems.
